questions.q: You collect 10,000 salaries instead of 100. What happens to the **histogram of individual salaries**?
options: It stays right-skewed; what becomes more precise is your estimate of the average salary
It becomes a normal bell curve, by the Central Limit Theorem
It becomes uniform
It becomes left-skewed
questions.why: The CLT is about the distribution of sample **means**, not the raw data. More data shows the skewed salary distribution more clearly; it does not reshape it. What shrinks is the standard error of the average.

questions.q: A survey of 400 customers finds an average basket of ₹520. In statistical language, ₹520 is a…
options: Parameter, because it describes customers
Statistic, calculated from the sample to estimate the unknown population parameter μ
Standard error
Population mean
questions.why: A statistic (here x̄) is computed from the sample; the parameter μ is the true average of all customers, which is usually unknown. We use statistics to estimate parameters. The standard error describes how much x̄ varies between samples.

questions.q: A fair die has mean 3.5 and SD 1.708. You roll 30 dice and average them. Using the CLT, roughly what is the probability that the average exceeds 4?
options: About 0.33, the chance a single die shows 5 or 6
About 0.39
About 0.055
About 0.0005
questions.why: SE = 1.708 / √30 = 0.312, z = (4 − 3.5) / 0.312 = 1.60, and P(z > 1.60) ≈ 0.055 (the exact answer by counting is 0.049). One third is the chance for a single die; averages are far more stable than individual rolls.

questions.q: A poll of **250** random customers estimates a share near 50%. What is the approximate 95% margin of error?
options: About ±3.1 percentage points
About ±3.2 percentage points
About ±12.4 percentage points
About ±6.2 percentage points
questions.why: SE = √(0.5 × 0.5 / 250) = 0.0316, and the margin is 1.96 × 0.0316 ≈ 0.062, so ±6.2 points. ±3.1 is the margin for 1,000 responses; ±3.2 is the SE alone, without the 1.96 multiplier.

questions.q: Two random polls each ask 1,000 people: one in a state of 15 lakh, one across a country of 140 crore. How do their margins of error compare?
options: The national poll's margin is far larger, because the population is about 1,000 times bigger
They are essentially the same (about ±3 points), because precision depends on sample size, not population size
The state poll is less precise because it covers a smaller share of people
The national poll needs 1,000 times more responses for the same margin
questions.why: The SE depends on the spread and on n, not on the population size, as long as the sample is a small fraction of it. Like tasting well-stirred soup, a spoonful works for any size of pot. A finite-population correction only matters when the sample is more than about 5 to 10% of the population.

questions.q: Basket values have SD ₹300. Roughly how many random receipts are needed for a standard error of ₹10?
questions.why: SE = σ / √n, so √n = 300 / 10 = 30 and n = 900. Stopping at 30 forgets to square; 300 confuses n with σ. Tripling precision from SE ₹30 (n = 100) costs nine times the data.

questions.q: An app survey gets 1 million responses, all from users who opened the app this week. The standard error of the average rating is tiny. What is the main risk?
options: Sampling bias: inactive and lapsed customers are missing, and bias does not shrink with n, so the answer can be precisely wrong
None; with a million responses the CLT guarantees an accurate answer
The standard error is too small to be calculated reliably
The ratings will not be normally distributed
questions.why: Standard error measures only random sampling error. A non-representative sample stays biased however large it is. The CLT cannot fix who was left out, and normality of individual ratings is not required for the average.

questions.q: In an interview: "Is n = 30 always enough for the Central Limit Theorem?" Which answer is best?
options: Yes, 30 is a mathematical threshold
Yes, as long as the raw data are normal
No, the CLT needs at least 1,000 observations
It is only a rough rule for moderately skewed data; very skewed or heavy-tailed data need much more, so simulate sample means from data shaped like yours to check
questions.why: 30 is a rule of thumb, not a theorem. Heavily skewed data need larger samples, and data with infinite variance break the CLT entirely. Simulating the distribution of means at your sample size is the honest check. If the raw data are already normal, means are normal at any n, so the rule is beside the point.
